title: Born in James Alley; singing in a quartet and church music
summary: Armstrong describes the back-of-town neighborhood of honky tonks, singing in a quartet at 12, church music and passing the hat for money.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, of course, you know, I was born in James Alley. That's back of town, we call it. That's in the rear of the city, where there's one street with everything. Honky tonks, churches, gambling, and everything. And I was just a kid, and I can remember all that. But I never did get heard. Then we moved in to Bedita and Franklin, where there was right to the heart of the little honky tonks, and even a schoolhouse. And we kids going to school didn't pay anything. We used to seeing a lot of loud cats, fights with pistols. It didn't bother you. It didn't even faze us, understand? And finally, I grew up to blow in one of those places myself, which I'm always around music. And I was playing in the honky tonks when Sturerville closed, see? Now, before that, at the age of 12, I was singing in a quartet. I always could sing, because my mother always took my sister and I to church. And this is what they call rock and roll today. We used to hear that same kind of music in sanctified churches, see? But they named it rock and roll, see what I mean? So quite naturally, I always could sing. And I was singing tenor at the time, young man. Put my hand behind my back and tear out, you know. And we'd go around the gamblers and the hustlers and pass our hat, you know, and have us sing for them. Money was money. Yeah, in 1915, a boy 12 years old would bring a dollar and a half of his take home. I would have divided up. That's a lot of money. I could help my sister, my mother, myself, to pay rent and then have a new shirt or new fat shoes or something, you know.
Did the kids you played with think you were about the best that they'd heard?
